content: Hi, I'm wondering if someone can point me in the direction of any work that's been done on reasoning about the cost of Boole programs as mentioned in the whitepaper+roadmap? I'm very interested in this topic and have been playing around with modeling cost semantics for a very basic Forth/EVM-inspired language and writing proofs for the cost of very basic programs. Curious what the approach will look like for Boole.

Right now there's no support for reasoning about the cost of programs. If you've been modeling cost semantics for stack-based languages, the ideas should translate well. Strata has a small-step operational semantics that could naturally be extended to track cumulative cost. So, t's an open area (as far as I know).

Thanks @Lydia Kondylidou I've been thinking about how one would define a cost semantics for Boole and I am dubious whether it is the right choice for reasoning about run-time and space-complexity in cslib. I have a few concerns:

1). Boole has "unbounded" types like int. This is an unrealistic way to model computation, akin to a word RAM with unbounded word size. It's going to be very weird to define the cost of adding two int's, as you're going to always need to know a bound on the size of the ints, so you're going to need to reason about the behavior of the program ahead of time. Also when you start composing programs you're going to get very messy bounds.

2). Boole has generic types (e.g. Map) but not basic dependent types like BitVec w. It would be nice if the model of computation itself could depend (in some uniform way) on the problem size parameter, like how in the word RAM model we assume that the word size is Theta(log n) -- or in general big enough to fit whatever "atoms" we're operating on. Analogously you should be able to write a procedure like:

procedure quadruple (a : BitVec w) : returns (c : BitVec w) {
  y := a + a
  c := y + y
}

Which should have cost 2 additions. I guess in Boole, to talk about the run-time of a function which quadruples an arbitrary length bit vector, you would have to write something like

procedure quadruple (a : Map int bool, size : int) returns (c : Map int bool) {
  call y := add(a, a, size)
  call c := add(y, y, size)
  assert [something about correctness]
}

This is really inconvenient, and I think to prove anything about run-time you're going to have to reason about how many keys of the Map you touch. Also note that in the prior example it's trivial to get a reasonable upper-bound on the space complexity of the procedure, but in this one it's not.

In summary I think it makes more sense to have finite types which grow depending on the problem size parameter instead of having unbounded types. Another example would be that it would be great to be able to write something like this:

procedure sum (a : StaticArray (uint m) n) : returns (c : (uint m)) {
...

(where uint m is an unsigned int of width m and staticarray is an array of length n) and be able to talk about the running time of sort as a function of m and n.

Do these concerns make sense or am I thinking about how you're planning on using Boole wrong?

These concerns are valid. Here is where Boole actually stands on each.

Cost semantics: None in Boole today. The decreases annotation is a termination measure only -- it generates non-negativity and strict-decrease VCs, not step counts. There is no operational semantics or cost model in the language.

int and word size: Agreed, int is the wrong primitive for complexity reasoning. Fixed-width types (bv32, bv64, etc.) exist but with concrete widths only. There is no bv w with a variable w.

Dependent types: Boole has none. quadruple (a : BitVec w) is not expressible. The Map int bool + size : int encoding you sketched is the closest approximation, and you are right that it loses the structural information needed for clean bounds.

StaticArray (uint m) n: Fixed-size array surface syntax is not yet implemented in Boole. Even once it is, N in [T; N] would be a concrete literal like [u32; 64], not a type parameter. Both m and n as variables requires dependent types.

Is correctness verification via SMT (cvc5) and the Lean backend still useful to you for the cslib use case, or does the absence of the above block the work entirely?

I guess I just thought that reasoning about the run-time of programs was one of the goals of cslib. I mean I know there's TimeM and now the query complexity stuff, but I thought the eventual goal was to get something more turnkey and complete

"In the longer run, we plan to complement this approach with heavier-weight methods that formalize complexity via explicit RAM and query models"
It is:) just not supported in Boole yet
Cool cool. So the goal would eventually be to augment Boole to be better suited for this purpose, like addressing the issues above?
Yes I believe this is the plan. Also connecting cslib pillar 1 and pillar 2 and addressing the question of how lean concepts can be represented in Boole. We are working on this:)

Ah, that's great. The point about the connection between Boole and Lean is something I've been thinking about too, i.e. instead of reasoning about correctness of algorithms in Boole directly, reasoning about their correspondence to some algorithm in Lean and then arguing directly about correctness there.

The run-time complexity issue is something I'm working on for my internship at MSR, so maybe we'll have something helpful to look at in the next couple months and could upstream to cslib. Please feel free to ping me in any discussions related to this or the Boole/Lean correspondence if it's not too much trouble
Sounds great! Will keep you up to date:)
